q: A front-desk sign is being revised before it is posted. Which sentence uses correct subject-verb agreement in inverted word order?
o: There is two forms that every new patient must sign at check-in.
On the counter sit two charts that still need a provider's signature.
Here is the signed consent forms for the two new patients.
There was several reasons that the appointment had to be moved.
w: When a sentence is inverted, find the subject after the verb. "Charts" is the subject of "sit," and both are plural, so "On the counter sit two charts" is correct.

n.0: In a "there" sentence the subject follows the verb. The subject is "forms" (plural), so it must be "There are."
n.2: The subject that follows the verb is "forms" (plural), so it must be "Here are the signed consent forms."
n.3: The subject is "reasons" (plural), which comes after the verb, so it must be "There were."

q: A student is editing a short article about a nursing school's admissions trends. Which sentence from the article uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: Twenty dollars are the fee that each applicant pays to submit a form.
The news about the new admission deadlines was posted on Monday.
A number of applicants has asked whether the essay is required.
The number of applicants to the program have doubled since 2020.
w: "News" ends in -s but is singular, so it takes "was." Remember: "the number of" is singular, "a number of" is plural, and a sum of money is singular.

n.0: An amount of money treated as one sum is singular: "Twenty dollars is the fee."
n.2: "A number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb: "A number of applicants have asked."
n.3: "The number of" is singular (it names one figure), so the verb must be "has doubled."

q: A preceptor is writing an incident note about an equipment check. Which sentence uses correct subject-verb agreement?
o: The nurse, along with two students, are checking the crash cart.
Neither the students nor the nurse are checking the crash cart today.
The nurse and two students, with the instructor, is checking the cart.
The nurse, as well as two students, is checking the crash cart.
w: Phrases such as "as well as," "along with" and "together with" do not make a subject plural. The subject is "nurse," so the verb is "is."

n.0: "Along with two students" is an intervening phrase, not part of the subject. The subject "nurse" is singular, so the verb must be "is."
n.1: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "nurse," which is singular, so it must be "is."
n.2: "The nurse and two students" is a compound subject joined by "and," which is plural, so the verb must be "are."

q: Read the sentence from a radiology department update: "The quality of the images from the older scanners have improved since the software update." Which revision corrects the agreement error?
o: Change "scanners" to "scanner."
Change "images" to "image."
Change "have improved" to "were improved."
Change "have improved" to "has improved."
w: The subject is "quality" (singular). "Of the images from the older scanners" is an intervening phrase, so the verb must be singular: "has improved."

n.0: "Scanners" is inside a prepositional phrase and is not the subject; the plural verb "have" would still disagree with "quality."
n.1: "Images" is also inside a prepositional phrase; the true subject "quality" still needs "has," so the error remains.
n.2: "Were" is still plural, so it does not agree with the singular subject "quality," and it changes the meaning to passive.

q: A supply clerk writes four notes for the end-of-day inventory report. Which note uses correct subject-verb agreement with an indefinite pronoun such as some, all, most or none?
o: Some of the patients in the waiting room is asking about the delay.
Most of the hand sanitizer in the supply room has been used this week.
All of the lab samples from this morning has been labeled and stored.
None of the water in the pitchers were changed during the night shift.
w: Some, any, none, all, most and more are singular or plural depending on the noun they refer to. "Sanitizer" is uncountable, so "most of the hand sanitizer has" is correct.

n.0: "Some" refers to "patients" (plural) here, so the verb must be "are asking."
n.2: "All" takes its number from the noun after "of." "Samples" is plural, so the verb must be "have been labeled."
n.3: "None" refers to "water," an uncountable noun, so it takes a singular verb: "was changed."

q: A charge nurse is reviewing sentences for a unit handbook. Which sentences use correct subject-verb agreement? Select all that apply.
o: Each of the new monitors come with a three-year warranty.
Everybody in both classes wants the exam moved to Friday.
The supply of masks in the storage rooms is running low.
The doctor's notes on the patient's progress was hard to read.
Either the pharmacist or the technicians are available after 6 p.m.
w: With "either...or," the verb agrees with the nearer subject ("technicians are"). "Everybody" is singular ("wants"). "Supply" is the subject of "is," not "masks" or "rooms."

n.0: "Each" is always singular, so it must be "Each of the new monitors comes"; "monitors" is inside the phrase "of the new monitors."
n.3: The subject is "notes" (plural); "on the patient's progress" is an intervening phrase, so the verb must be "were."

q: A volunteer coordinator drafts four sentences for a hospital welcome packet. Which sentence contains an error in subject-verb agreement?
o: The bag of IV fluid hanging by the bed is due to be replaced.
Neither of the two applicants has submitted a transcript yet.
There are a clipboard and two pens at the front desk for visitors.
Each of the patients on the third floor have a call button.
w: "Each" is always singular, so the verb must be "has": "Each of the patients on the third floor has a call button." The plural "patients" sits inside a prepositional phrase.

n.0: This sentence is correct: the subject "bag" is singular and takes "is"; "of IV fluid hanging by the bed" does not change it.
n.1: This sentence is correct: "neither" used as a pronoun is singular, so "has submitted" agrees.
n.2: This sentence is correct: the subject after the verb is compound ("a clipboard and two pens"), so the plural "are" agrees.

q: Read the paragraph from a clinic notice. (1) The clinic's new hours begin next week. (2) Patients who arrive after 5 p.m. will be seen by the on-call provider. (3) A list of the providers' schedules are posted at the front desk. (4) Questions about the change go to the office manager. Which sentence contains a subject-verb agreement error?
o: Sentence 4
Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 1
w: In sentence 3 the subject is "list" (singular), so the verb must be "is posted." "Of the providers' schedules" is an intervening phrase.

n.0: The subject "questions" is plural and "go" is plural; "about the change" does not affect agreement.
n.1: "Patients" is plural, and "will be seen" works for any subject; the clause "who arrive" agrees with "patients."
n.3: "Hours" is plural and "begin" is a plural verb, so sentence 1 agrees.

q: A student is editing a reflection paper about a clinical skills lab. Which sentence from the paper uses pronoun case correctly?
o: Him and his sister both applied to the nursing program this year.
Between you and me, the new skills schedule is an improvement.
The instructor asked Maria and I to demonstrate the bed transfer.
The award went to Devon and myself for the hand-hygiene project.
w: "Between" is a preposition, and the object of a preposition takes the objective case: "between you and me."

n.0: "Him and his sister" is the subject, so the subjective case is needed: "He and his sister."
n.2: "Maria and I" is the object of "asked," so the objective case is needed: "asked Maria and me." Drop "Maria and" to test: "asked me."
n.3: "Myself" is reflexive and has no antecedent in the sentence; the object of "to" needs "me": "to Devon and me."

q: A clinic receptionist is writing questions for a new front-desk guide. Which sentence uses who or whom correctly?
o: The student whom earned the top score will speak at graduation.
Whom do you think will be named the new charge nurse?
To whom should I send the completed insurance forms?
Whom is responsible for the night count of controlled drugs?
w: "Whom" is the objective form. In "To whom should I send," the pronoun is the object of the preposition "to" (send them to him), so "whom" is correct.

n.0: The pronoun is the subject of "earned" (she earned), so it must be "who."
n.1: Ignore "do you think": the pronoun is the subject of "will be named" (he will be named), so it must be "Who."
n.3: The pronoun is the subject of "is responsible" (he is responsible), so it must be "Who."

q: A nursing club is printing a flyer about clinical placements. Which sentence on the flyer uses the pronouns "we" and "us" correctly?
o: Us students were asked to arrive by 6:30 a.m. for clinicals.
The new policy was explained to we volunteers on Monday.
The instructor gave us students extra time on the dosage exam.
Several of we applicants had questions about the essay prompt.
w: Drop the noun to test: "The instructor gave us extra time" is correct, so "gave us students" is correct. "Us" is the indirect object of "gave."

n.0: Drop "students": "Us were asked" is wrong. The phrase is the subject, so it must be "We students."
n.1: Drop "volunteers": "explained to we" is wrong. The object of "to" needs "us volunteers."
n.3: "Of" is a preposition, so its object needs the objective case: "several of us applicants."

q: A lab manager is reviewing safety notes before they are posted. Which sentence has a pronoun that agrees with its antecedent in number and person?
o: The lab and the pharmacy will extend its hours in December.
If a student wants to pass, you have to practice every day.
All of the incubators must have its filters changed every month.
Each of the vials must be inspected for cracks before it is used.
w: "Each" is singular, and a vial is a thing, so the singular pronoun "it" agrees in number and person.

n.0: Two antecedents joined by "and" are plural, so the pronoun must be "their hours."
n.1: The sentence shifts from third person ("a student") to second person ("you"); keep the same person throughout.
n.2: "All" refers to "incubators" (plural) here, so the pronoun must be plural: "their filters."

q: Read the sentence from a patient's visit summary: "When Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, he explained the test results." Which revision removes the unclear pronoun reference?
o: When Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, they explained the new test results.
Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, and he explained all of the new test results.
When Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, he carefully explained the test results.
When Dr. Okafor met with Mr. Hale, the doctor explained the test results.
w: A pronoun must point to one clear antecedent. Replacing "he" with "the doctor" shows that Dr. Okafor explained the results.

n.0: "They" is still unclear (both men? someone else?) and does not identify who explained the results.
n.1: Joining the clauses with "and" keeps the same ambiguous "he" with two possible antecedents.
n.2: Adding "carefully" does not fix the problem: "he" could still mean either man.

q: A student is citing a hospital handbook in a short report. Which sentence avoids a vague pronoun reference?
o: In the employee handbook, they state that meal breaks last thirty minutes.
They say in the employee handbook that meal breaks last thirty minutes.
The handbook and the shift schedule both list breaks, and it says they last thirty minutes.
The employee handbook states that meal breaks last thirty minutes.
w: Every pronoun needs a clear antecedent. Making "the employee handbook" the subject removes the vague "they" or "it."

n.0: "They" is vague: the handbook is a thing, and no people have been named.
n.1: "They" has no antecedent; the sentence never names who "they" are.
n.2: "It" could mean the handbook or the shift schedule, so the reference is unclear even though both nouns are named.

q: A nurse is writing a short thank-you note to a colleague. Which sentence uses a reflexive pronoun correctly?
o: My lab partner and myself presented the case study on Monday.
Please return the signed form to Ms. Park or myself by Friday.
The residents organized the whole fundraiser theirselves this year.
Kendra reminded herself to recheck the dosage before charting it.
w: A reflexive pronoun is correct when its antecedent is in the same clause. "Herself" refers back to "Kendra," who did the reminding.

n.0: "Myself" cannot be part of a subject; the subjective case is needed: "My lab partner and I."
n.1: "Myself" has no antecedent in this sentence; the object of "to" needs "me": "to Ms. Park or me."
n.2: "Theirselves" is nonstandard; the reflexive form is "themselves."

q: Read the sentence from a shift report: "The charge nurse divided the six patients between Tomas and I so that each of us had three." Which revision corrects the pronoun error?
o: Change "had" to "have."
Change "I" to "me."
Change "us" to "we."
Change "I" to "myself."
w: "Between" is a preposition, so both of its objects take the objective case: "between Tomas and me."

n.0: "Each" is singular, so "had" (or "has") is right; "have" adds a tense shift and does not fix "between Tomas and I."
n.2: "Us" is correct as the object of the preposition "of"; "each of we" would create a new error.
n.3: "Myself" needs an antecedent in the sentence that refers to the same person; the object of "between" needs "me."

q: A pharmacy intern is drafting a patient handout. Which sentence contains an inappropriate shift in pronoun person?
o: We volunteers should bring our badges to every shift this month.
Applicants should check their email often, since the school sends updates there.
If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember it.
When one reads a drug label, you should check the expiration date first.
w: "One" is third person, but "you" is second person. Keep one point of view: "When you read a drug label, you should..."

n.0: This sentence stays in first person plural: "we" and "our."
n.1: This sentence is consistent: "applicants" and "their" are both third person plural.
n.2: This sentence stays in second person throughout ("you" and the implied "you" of "take").

q: An instructor is grading sentences on a grammar quiz for first-year nursing students. Which sentences use pronouns correctly? Select all that apply.
o: Whom should the front desk call if the results are late?
The tutor helped Grace and myself with dosage problems.
The award was shared by Mei and her.
Dev and me will cover the weekend shifts in March.
Each of the clinics posted its holiday hours online.
w: "Each" is singular, so "its" agrees. "By Mei and her" uses the objective case after the preposition "by." "Whom" is the object of "call" (the desk should call him).

n.1: "Myself" has no antecedent in the sentence; the object of "helped" needs "me": "Grace and me."
n.3: "Dev and me" is the subject, so it needs the subjective case: "Dev and I will cover."

q: Read the sentence from a staff memo: "The pharmacist told the technician that her shift had been changed." Which revision makes the pronoun reference clear?
o: The pharmacist told the technician that her shift had now been changed.
The pharmacist and the technician were told that her shift changed.
The pharmacist told the technician that her own shift had been changed.
The pharmacist told the technician, "Your shift has been changed."
w: Turning the report into a direct quotation makes "your" refer clearly to the technician, the person being spoken to.

n.0: Adding "now" leaves "her" ambiguous; it could still mean the pharmacist's shift or the technician's.
n.1: "Her" now has two possible antecedents in the subject, so the reference is still unclear.
n.2: Adding "own" does not help: "her own" could still mean the pharmacist's shift or the technician's.

q: Read the paragraph from a clinic newsletter. (1) The Riverside Clinic opened a second location this spring. (2) Its new site offers evening hours for working families. (3) Patients may book appointments at either location online. (4) Dr. Liu and myself will divide our time between the two offices. Which sentence contains a pronoun error?
o: Sentence 4
Sentence 3
Sentence 1
Sentence 2
w: In sentence 4, "myself" is part of the subject and has no antecedent; the subjective case is needed: "Dr. Liu and I will divide our time."

n.1: Sentence 3 has no pronoun error; "either location" is singular and correctly used.
n.2: Sentence 1 contains no pronoun error; it has no pronoun at all.
n.3: "Its" is the correct possessive for the clinic (one organization), with no apostrophe.

q: A nursing student is proofreading her clinical journal. Which sentence from the journal uses the correct form of an irregular verb?
o: She has wrote three care plans for the pediatric rotation.
By the time I arrived, my preceptor had went to the meeting.
The new aide has already taken the medication safety course.
I seen the updated schedule posted near the break room.
w: "Take" is irregular: take, took, taken. A helping verb ("has") takes the past participle "taken."

n.0: "Has" needs the past participle "written"; "wrote" is the simple past.
n.1: "Had" needs the past participle "gone"; "went" is the simple past and cannot follow a helping verb.
n.3: "Seen" is a past participle and needs a helping verb ("have seen"); otherwise use the simple past "saw."

q: A home health aide is writing up visit notes. Which sentence uses "lie" or "lay" correctly?
o: After the procedure, the patient laid on his side for an hour.
Please lie the clean linens on the bottom shelf of the cart.
Yesterday, Ana lay down for a nap after her long night shift.
The dog has laid by the front door all afternoon long.
w: "Lie" (to recline, no object) is lie, lay, lain. "Yesterday ... lay down" is the past tense of "lie," so it is correct.

n.0: The patient is reclining (no object), so the verb is "lie"; its past tense is "lay," not "laid."
n.1: Putting linens down takes an object, so the verb is "lay": "Please lay the clean linens."
n.3: The dog is reclining, so the verb is "lie"; its past participle is "lain": "has lain."

q: A certified nursing assistant is charting a routine check. Which sentence keeps verb tense consistent?
o: The aide checked the patient's temperature and recorded it in the chart.
The aide checked the patient's temperature and records it in the chart.
The aide checks the patient's temperature and recorded it in the chart.
The aide checks the patient's temperature and had recorded it in the chart.
w: Both actions happened in the same past visit, so both verbs stay in the simple past: "checked ... recorded."

n.1: The sentence shifts from past ("checked") to present ("records") for two actions in the same visit.
n.2: The sentence shifts from present ("checks") to past ("recorded") with no reason for the change.
n.3: The past perfect "had recorded" places the recording before the checking, which is illogical, and it shifts tense.

q: A surgical unit's family liaison is writing an update. Which sentence uses the past perfect tense correctly to show which action happened first?
o: The surgeon had finished the procedure by the time the family arrived.
The surgeon had finished the procedure by the time the family arrives.
The surgeon finishes the procedure by the time the family had arrived.
The surgeon has finished the procedure by the time the family arrived.
w: The past perfect (had + past participle) marks the earlier of two past actions. The procedure ended first, then the family arrived.

n.1: "Arrives" is present tense, which clashes with "had finished"; both events are in the past.
n.2: The tenses are reversed: the earlier action (finishing) needs the past perfect, and the later one the simple past.
n.3: The present perfect "has finished" does not fit a completed past time frame set by "arrived"; use "had finished."

q: A physical therapy assistant is writing notes after a session. Which sentence uses "rise" or "raise" correctly?
o: Prices for the required nursing textbooks have raised every semester.
The therapist asked the patient to rise his arm above his head.
The patient's temperature rose overnight, so we called the doctor.
The aide raised from her chair when the surgeon entered the room.
w: "Rise" (rise, rose, risen) has no object; "raise" (raise, raised, raised) takes one. A temperature goes up by itself, so "rose" is correct.

n.0: Prices go up on their own (no object), so the verb must be "risen": "have risen."
n.1: Lifting an arm takes an object ("his arm"), so the verb must be "raise."
n.3: Getting up has no object, so the verb must be "rose" (past of "rise").

q: A clinic receptionist is writing instructions for the waiting area. Which sentence uses "sit" and "set" correctly?
o: He set the tray on the table and sat beside his mother.
Please set in the chair by the window until your name is called.
The patient has set in the waiting room for over two hours.
She sat the specimen cup on the counter next to the sink.
w: "Set" (set, set, set) means to place something and takes an object (the tray). "Sit" (sit, sat, sat) has no object (he sat).

n.1: A person resting in a chair needs "sit" (no object); "set" means to place something.
n.2: The patient is seated (no object), so the verb must be "sat": "has sat."
n.3: Placing a cup takes an object, so the verb must be "set": "She set the specimen cup."

q: Read the sentence from a pharmacy incident report: "If the order had been clearer, the pharmacy could of filled it on time." Which revision corrects the verb error?
o: Change "could of filled" to "could have filled" and "had been" to "would have been."
Change "could of filled" to "could have filled."
Change "had been" to "was."
Change "could of filled" to "could had filled."
w: "Could of" is a mishearing of "could've." The correct form is "could have" + past participle: "could have filled."

n.0: This fixes "could of" but adds a new error: the if-clause of a past unreal condition takes "had been," not "would have been."
n.2: "Had been" is correct for a past condition that did not happen, and the "could of" error would remain.
n.3: "Could" is a helping verb and must be followed by the base form "have"; "could had filled" is ungrammatical.

q: A student is writing a persuasive paragraph for a nursing program application and must use formal written English. Which sentence uses the subjunctive mood correctly?
o: If I was the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
If I were the instructor, I will allow one retake per exam.
If I would be the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
If I were the instructor, I would allow one retake per exam.
w: For an unreal or hypothetical condition, formal English uses "were" for all subjects and "would" in the main clause.

n.0: A condition contrary to fact takes the subjunctive "were" in formal writing, not "was."
n.1: An unreal "if I were" condition pairs with "would," not the future "will."
n.2: "Would" belongs in the result clause, not the if-clause; use "If I were."

q: A writing tutor reviews sentences from nursing students' reflection papers. Which sentences use irregular verbs correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The pipes in the old wing had froze before the heat came back on.
The intern has chose a specialty in pediatric nursing.
Ms. Reyes has led the infection control team since 2021.
The patient has already swum two laps in the therapy pool.
The phone rung three times before anyone at the desk answered.
By noon, the volunteers had drunk all of the bottled water.
w: Drink, drank, drunk; lead, led, led; swim, swam, swum. Each helping verb (had, has) is paired with the correct past participle.

n.0: After "had," use the past participle "frozen": "had frozen."
n.1: After "has," use the past participle "chosen": "has chosen."
n.4: The simple past of "ring" is "rang"; "rung" is the past participle and needs a helping verb.

q: Read the paragraph from a scholarship essay. (1) Last spring, Keisha volunteered at a free clinic in her town. (2) She checks in patients and took their blood pressure. (3) The experience showed her how much she enjoyed patient care. (4) By June, she had decided to apply to nursing school. Which sentence contains an unnecessary shift in verb tense?
o: Sentence 4
Sentence 3
Sentence 1
Sentence 2
w: Sentence 2 shifts from present ("checks") to past ("took") while describing the same past events; it should read "She checked in patients and took..."

n.0: "Had decided" is past perfect, correctly marking a decision completed by a past point ("By June").
n.1: "Showed" and "enjoyed" are both simple past, consistent with the rest of the paragraph.
n.2: "Volunteered" is simple past, which matches "last spring."

q: Read the sentence from a quality report: "Since the new reminder policy started, the clinic has saw fewer missed appointments." Which revision corrects the verb error?
o: Change "has saw" to "seen."
Change "has saw" to "have seen."
Change "has saw" to "has seen."
Change "has saw" to "had saw."
w: Two steps: "since" calls for the present perfect, and a singular subject ("clinic") takes "has" + the past participle "seen."

n.0: A past participle cannot stand alone as the main verb; it needs "has."
n.1: "Seen" is right, but "clinic" is singular, so the helping verb must stay "has."
n.3: "Saw" is the simple past and cannot follow any helping verb; the participle is "seen."

q: A hospital's staff profile page is being edited. Which sentence uses verb tense correctly with the phrase "since 2019"?
o: Dr. Patel has worked at the hospital in 2019.
Dr. Patel works at the hospital since 2019.
Dr. Patel is working at the hospital since 2019.
Dr. Patel has worked at the hospital since 2019.
w: The present perfect (has/have + past participle) shows an action that began in the past and continues now: "has worked ... since 2019."

n.0: The present perfect does not pair with a finished, specific past time such as "in 2019"; use "worked in 2019."
n.1: "Since" marks an action that began in the past and continues, which needs the present perfect "has worked."
n.2: The present progressive does not fit an ongoing span that began at a past point; use "has worked" or "has been working."

q: A nursing student is revising the opening of a clinical narrative. Which sentence is written correctly, with no dangling modifier?
o: Walking into the clinic, it was clear that the lobby was full.
Walking into the clinic, the crowd in the lobby surprised her.
Walking into the clinic, the lobby looked crowded to Rosa.
Walking into the clinic, Rosa saw that the lobby was crowded.
w: An introductory participial phrase must be followed by the person or thing doing the action. Rosa was walking into the clinic, so "Rosa" must come right after the comma.

n.0: "It" cannot do the walking; the person who walked in never appears as the subject.
n.1: The subject after the phrase is "the crowd," so the sentence says the crowd was walking into the clinic.
n.2: The phrase "Walking into the clinic" is followed by "the lobby," so the sentence says the lobby was walking.

q: A clinic manager wants to say that no more than two nurses are scheduled on weekends. Which sentence places the limiting word so that it states this meaning most clearly?
o: The clinic only schedules two nurses on weekends.
Only the clinic schedules two nurses on weekends.
The clinic schedules only two nurses on weekends.
The clinic schedules two nurses only on weekends.
w: A limiting word such as only, just, nearly or almost goes directly before the word it limits. To limit the number, "only" goes before "two nurses."

n.0: Placed before the verb, "only" limits "schedules" (it schedules and does nothing else), not the number two.
n.1: Placed before "the clinic," "only" means no other place schedules two nurses, which is a different meaning.
n.3: Placed before "on weekends," "only" means nurses are scheduled on weekends and not on weekdays.

q: A student is editing a peer's care-plan summary. Which sentence uses adjectives and adverbs correctly?
o: After a night of rest, Jordan felt well enough to go to class.
The new graduate handled the emergency calm and careful.
The cafeteria soup tasted differently after the new cook started.
The team did real good on the state safety inspection this year.
w: "Well" can be an adjective meaning "in good health," so "felt well" is correct after the linking verb "felt."

n.1: "Calm" and "careful" describe how she handled it, so they modify a verb and must be adverbs: "calmly and carefully."
n.2: "Tasted" is a linking verb here, so it takes an adjective that describes the soup: "tasted different."
n.3: "Did" is an action verb, so it needs the adverb "well"; "real" should also be the adverb "really."

q: A pharmacy student is comparing products in a study guide. Which sentence uses a comparative or superlative form correctly?
o: The night shift is more busier than the day shift on most weekends.
Of the three dressings, the foam one is the least painful to remove.
Of the two inhalers, the blue one is the most effective for her asthma.
Of the three textbooks, this one is the better choice for anatomy.
w: With three or more items, use the superlative (-est, most, least). Three dressings are compared, so "least painful" is correct.

n.0: "More busier" is a double comparative; use "busier" alone.
n.2: Comparing exactly two items calls for the comparative: "the more effective."
n.3: Comparing three or more items calls for the superlative: "the best choice."

q: A quality-improvement report summarizes changes in a clinic. Which sentence uses "fewer" or "less" correctly?
o: There were fewer complaints after the new check-in system began.
The new menu offers less calories per serving than the old one did.
The weekend shift now runs with less staff members than before.
The clinic saw less patients this month than it did last month.
w: Use "fewer" with countable plural nouns (complaints, patients, calories, staff members) and "less" with uncountable nouns (water, sodium, time).

n.1: "Calories" can be counted, so the sentence needs "fewer calories."
n.2: "Staff members" is a countable plural, so it needs "fewer staff members" ("less staff" alone would be fine).
n.3: "Patients" can be counted, so the sentence needs "fewer patients."

q: A community health volunteer is writing a short event summary. Which sentence places the modifier "with large print" correctly?
o: The volunteer handed out flyers to the families with large print.
The volunteer with large print handed out flyers to the families.
The volunteer handed out flyers with large print to the families.
With large print, the volunteer handed out flyers to the families.
w: A modifier belongs next to the word it describes. The large print is on the flyers, so the phrase must follow "flyers."

n.0: Placed after "families," the phrase seems to describe the families, not the flyers.
n.1: Placed after "volunteer," the phrase describes the volunteer instead of the flyers.
n.3: Placed at the start, the phrase seems to describe the volunteer, who is not printed.

q: A home care agency is revising a client letter. Which sentence is written in standard English with no double negative?
o: The aide hadn't scarcely finished charting when the call light came on.
The patient can't hardly sit up in bed without help from staff.
The pharmacy didn't have any of the brand-name tablets in stock.
There isn't no reason for the patient to skip the follow-up visit.
w: One negative is enough. "Didn't" is negative and "any" is neutral, so the sentence is correct.

n.0: "Scarcely" is negative in meaning, so "hadn't scarcely" is a double negative; use "had scarcely."
n.1: "Hardly" is already negative, so "can't hardly" is a double negative; use "can hardly."
n.3: "Isn't" and "no" are two negatives; use "There is no reason" or "There isn't any reason."

q: Read the sentence from a discharge summary: "After reviewing the lab results, a new medication was ordered." Which revision corrects the dangling modifier?
o: After reviewing the lab results, the doctor's decision was to order a new medication.
After reviewing the lab results, the doctor's order called for a new medication.
After reviewing the lab results, a new medication was ordered by the doctor.
After reviewing the lab results, the doctor ordered a new medication.
w: The person who reviewed the results (the doctor) must be the subject right after the introductory phrase.

n.0: The subject after the comma is "decision," and a decision cannot review lab results; "doctor's" is only a possessive.
n.1: The subject after the comma is "order," so the sentence says the order reviewed the results; the doctor must be the subject.
n.2: The subject after the comma is still "a new medication," so the sentence still says the medication reviewed the results.

q: A patient satisfaction survey summary is being edited. Which sentence uses an adjective correctly after a linking verb?
o: The coffee in the staff break room tastes bitter today.
The infant is breathing good now that the fever has broken.
Their new manager seems nicely, and the staff likes her a lot.
The cafeteria food tastes differently since the new cook started.
w: Linking verbs (taste, seem, feel, look, smell) connect the subject to an adjective that describes it: the coffee tastes bitter.

n.1: "Breathing" is an action, so it needs the adverb "well," not the adjective "good."
n.2: "Seems" is a linking verb, so it takes the adjective "nice," not the adverb "nicely."
n.3: "Tastes" links the food to a description, so it needs the adjective "different," not the adverb.

q: An instructor is checking sentences from student case studies. Which sentences use modifiers correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The pharmacist spoke so quietly that the patient asked her to repeat herself.
To pass the licensing exam, careful studying is needed.
Nearly all of the students passed the skills check on the first try.
Of the two job offers, Darnell accepted the best one.
Having finished her charting, Mia clocked out and drove home.
w: Mia is the one who finished charting; "quietly" is an adverb modifying "spoke"; "nearly" sits right before "all," the word it limits.

n.1: The infinitive phrase dangles: "studying" cannot pass an exam. A person must be the subject: "To pass the exam, you need to study carefully."
n.3: Two offers call for the comparative "the better one," not the superlative "best."

q: A clinic's annual report is being proofread. Which sentence chooses correctly between "number" and "amount" or between "among" and "between"?
o: The large amount of patients in the lobby slowed down check-in.
The profits were split evenly among the two clinic owners.
A large number of applicants missed the deadline this year.
The amount of volunteers at the blood drive doubled this year.
w: "Number" goes with countable nouns (applicants), "amount" with uncountable ones (water). "Between" is for two; "among" for three or more.

n.0: "Patients" can be counted, so the sentence needs "number," not "amount."
n.1: "Among" is for three or more; with two owners use "between."
n.3: "Volunteers" are countable, so the sentence needs "number of volunteers."

q: Read the paragraph from a patient success story. (1) Hoping to lower her blood pressure, Mrs. Diaz began walking every morning. (2) She walked more slowly than her neighbor but went farther. (3) After three weeks, her readings were lower than before. (4) Encouraged by the results, the walks became longer. Which sentence contains a dangling modifier?
o: Sentence 3
Sentence 1
Sentence 4
Sentence 2
w: In sentence 4, "Encouraged by the results" is followed by "the walks," so the walks seem encouraged. Fix: "Encouraged by the results, Mrs. Diaz made her walks longer."

n.0: "Lower" correctly compares two things (readings now and before); there is no introductory modifier to dangle.
n.1: "Hoping to lower her blood pressure" is followed by "Mrs. Diaz," the person who was hoping, so the modifier is correct.
n.3: "More slowly" correctly compares two people with an adverb, and "farther" correctly refers to physical distance.

q: A long-term care facility is updating its training description for new aides. Which sentence uses parallel structure?
o: New aides learn to take vital signs, to record intake, and how to reposition patients.
New aides learn to take vital signs, record intake, and reposition patients.
New aides learn to take vital signs, recording intake, and to reposition patients.
New aides learn taking vital signs, to record intake, and repositioning patients.
w: Items in a series must share one grammatical form. After "learn to," the three base verbs (take, record, reposition) are parallel.

n.0: The third item switches from an infinitive ("to record") to a "how to" phrase, so the list is not parallel.
n.2: "Recording" is a gerund placed between two infinitives, which breaks the parallel pattern.
n.3: The list mixes gerunds ("taking," "repositioning") with an infinitive ("to record").

q: A community college brochure describes a nursing pathway program. Which sentence uses "not only...but also" correctly?
o: The program not only trains nurses but also it places them in local clinics.
The program trains not only nurses but also places them in local clinics.
The program not only trains nurses but also places them in local clinics.
Not only does the program train nurses but also places them in local clinics.
w: Correlative pairs must be followed by matching elements. Here each part is followed by a verb phrase: "not only trains ... but also places."

n.0: "But also" is followed by a full clause ("it places"), while "not only" is followed by a verb; the two parts do not match.
n.1: "Not only" precedes a noun ("nurses") but "but also" precedes a verb ("places"); each part needs the same form.
n.3: "Not only" introduces an inverted clause, but "but also" introduces a bare verb phrase, so the pair is not parallel.

q: Read the sentence from a transportation notice: "Due to the fact that the main road was closed, the shuttle arrived late to the clinic." Which revision is most concise while keeping the full meaning?
o: Due to the main road closure, the shuttle arrived late.
Because the main road was closed, the shuttle arrived late to the clinic.
The main road was closed, the shuttle arrived late to the clinic.
Since the main road was closed off, the shuttle was late in arriving to the clinic.
w: "Due to the fact that" is a wordy way to say "because." Replacing it keeps every detail and the correct structure.

n.0: This version drops "to the clinic," so it loses part of the original meaning.
n.2: This version is shorter but joins two independent clauses with only a comma, creating a comma splice.
n.3: This version is wordier than the original idea needs ("closed off," "was late in arriving").

q: A hospital volunteer guide is being edited for wordiness. Which sentence is written without a redundant phrase?
o: The two outpatient clinics are located in close proximity to each other.
Please repeat the instructions again for the new patients in the lobby.
Every visitor must sign in at the front desk before going upstairs.
The clinic offers a free gift to every new patient who enrolls this month.
w: Concise writing removes words that repeat meaning. The correct sentence has no redundant pair such as "repeat again," "free gift" or "close proximity."

n.0: "Proximity" already means "closeness," so "close proximity" is redundant; "close to each other" is enough.
n.1: "Repeat" already means "say again," so "repeat ... again" is redundant.
n.3: A gift is free by definition, so "free gift" is redundant.

q: A health blog compares two urgent care centers. Which sentence makes a logical, parallel comparison?
o: Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than those at Eastside Clinic.
Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than the staff at Eastside Clinic.
Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than at Eastside Clinic's.
Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than Eastside Clinic is.
w: A comparison must set like things side by side: wait times at one clinic versus wait times ("those") at the other.

n.1: This compares wait times to the staff, two unlike things; the comparison needs "those at Eastside Clinic."
n.2: The possessive "Eastside Clinic's" leaves the noun it owns unstated, so the comparison is garbled.
n.3: This still compares wait times (plural) with a clinic (singular), which is illogical.

q: A clinic's patient portal page explains check-in options. Which sentence uses "either...or" with parallel elements?
o: Patients can either check in on the website or at the front desk.
Either patients can check in on the website or at the front desk.
Patients either can check in on the website or the front desk.
Patients can check in either on the website or at the front desk.
w: Place "either" and "or" directly before matching elements. Here both introduce a prepositional phrase: "on the website" and "at the front desk."

n.0: "Either" comes before a verb ("check in") but "or" comes before a prepositional phrase, so the pair is not parallel.
n.1: "Either" comes before a full clause but "or" comes before a phrase, so the two parts do not match.
n.2: "Either" precedes a verb phrase while "or" precedes a noun ("the front desk"), which is not parallel.

q: Read the sentence from a hospital policy summary: "The new policy is meant to reduce wait times, improving patient satisfaction, and to lower costs." Which revision corrects the faulty parallelism?
o: Change "to lower" to "lowering."
Change "to reduce" to "reducing."
Change "improving" to "to improve."
Delete the word "and" before "to lower."
w: Two of the three items are infinitives (to reduce, to lower). Changing "improving" to "to improve" makes all three match.

n.0: This leaves "to reduce" as an infinitive while the other two items are gerunds, so the list is still mixed.
n.1: This leaves "to lower" as an infinitive while the other two items are gerunds, so the list is still mixed.
n.3: Removing "and" does not change the forms of the items and also leaves the series without its conjunction.

q: A state board newsletter is being edited for concise wording. Which sentence is the most concise version that keeps the full meaning?
o: To renew a license, it is required that nurses in this state complete 24 hours of continuing education.
To renew, nurses must complete 24 hours.
In order to renew a license, nurses in this state must complete 24 hours of continuing education.
To renew a license, nurses in this state must complete 24 hours of continuing education.
w: Concise does not mean shortest. The best version removes padding ("in order to," "it is required that") and keeps every detail.

n.0: "It is required that" is a wordy construction; "must" says the same thing more directly.
n.1: This version drops what is renewed, the state, and the type of hours, so it loses meaning.
n.2: "In order to" adds words without adding meaning; "to" alone is enough.

q: A nursing school's simulation lab description is being proofread. Which sentence uses "both...and" with parallel elements?
o: The simulation lab is both useful for students and inexpensive to run.
The simulation lab is useful both for students and inexpensive to run.
The simulation lab is both useful for students and costs little to run.
The simulation lab both is useful for students and inexpensive to run.
w: "Both" and "and" are each followed by an adjective phrase: "useful for students" and "inexpensive to run."

n.1: "Both" now precedes a prepositional phrase ("for students") but "and" precedes an adjective.
n.2: "Both" is followed by an adjective ("useful") but "and" by a verb ("costs"), so the pair is not parallel.
n.3: "Both" is placed before the verb "is," but "and" is followed by an adjective; the two parts do not match.

q: A clinical instructor is reviewing four sentences from a student handbook draft. Which sentence is written with parallel structure?
o: The applicant was praised for her punctuality, her empathy, and for being skilled.
The checklist asks staff to wash hands, wear gloves, and dispose of sharps safely.
Volunteers may greet visitors, deliver flowers, or they can read to patients.
The course teaches students how to splint a fracture and controlling bleeding.
w: All three items after "to" are base verbs (wash, wear, dispose), so the series is parallel.

n.0: Two nouns ("her punctuality," "her empathy") are followed by a gerund phrase with a repeated "for"; it should be "and her clinical skill."
n.2: The first two items are verb phrases, but the third is a full clause ("they can read"); it should be "or read to patients."
n.3: "How to splint" is paired with the gerund "controlling"; it should be "how to splint a fracture and control bleeding."

q: Read the sentence from a research summary: "The two surgeons collaborated together on a new protocol that cut postoperative infections by 30 percent." Which word should be deleted to remove a redundancy?
o: together
new
postoperative
two
w: "Collaborate" means "work together," so "collaborated together" repeats the idea. Deleting "together" removes the redundancy.

n.1: "New" tells the reader the protocol was recently created; it is not implied by any other word.
n.2: "Postoperative" names which infections were cut; deleting it would make the claim broader than the study.
n.3: "Collaborate" implies at least two people, but "two" states exactly how many surgeons, so it adds information.

q: A grant proposal for a nursing assistant program states its goals. Which version is both parallel and concise?
o: The goals of the program are training aides, to place them in jobs, and supporting them after they are hired.
The goals of the program are to train aides, to place them in jobs, and to support them after hiring.
The goals of the program are to train aides, to place them in jobs, and to support and help them after hiring.
The goals of the program are to train aides, placing them in jobs, and to support them after hiring.
w: Two checks: the three goals share one form (to train, to place, to support), and no words repeat the same meaning.

n.0: The series mixes gerunds ("training," "supporting") with an infinitive ("to place").
n.2: The list is parallel, but "support and help" repeats one idea, so the sentence is not concise.
n.3: "Placing" is a gerund between two infinitives, so the series is not parallel.

q: A nursing student is emailing her pharmacology professor to ask for a meeting about a failed exam. Which sentence is most appropriate for this audience and purpose?
o: I hereby request an audience at your earliest convenience regarding my examination.
I will stop by your office at noon tomorrow to go over my exam.
I would like to schedule a meeting to discuss my recent exam results.
I was hoping we might talk soon about a few things from class.
w: An email to a professor calls for formal, polite language that states the purpose clearly: a meeting about exam results.

n.0: "I hereby request an audience" is inflated, stiff wording; a clear, polite request suits an email to a professor.
n.1: The writer announces a visit instead of asking for one, which is presumptuous toward the professor.
n.3: The request is vague ("a few things from class"); it never says the meeting is about the exam.

q: A clinic is writing a handout for patients who have no medical training. Which sentence is best suited to these readers?
o: Pt should obtain BP readings BID and document all of the findings.
Check your blood pressure at the same time each morning and evening.
Check your systolic and diastolic pressure each morning and evening.
Patients with hypertension should monitor their BP readings diurnally.
w: Plain language for a lay audience uses everyday words, short sentences and clear actions, without jargon or slang.

n.0: Clinical abbreviations (Pt, BP, BID) are jargon meant for health professionals, not patients.
n.2: The action is clear, but "systolic" and "diastolic" are medical terms a lay reader may not know.
n.3: "Hypertension," "BP" and "diurnally" are technical terms a lay reader may not understand.

q: A student is writing a formal research paper on sleep and academic performance. Which sentence is most appropriate for this paper?
o: Students who sleep fewer than six hours tend to earn lower grades.
Research shows that students who skimp on sleep see their grades tank.
Students who don't get enough sleep tend to earn lower grades.
You'd be surprised how much your sleep affects your final grades.
w: Formal academic writing uses third person, precise wording, no contractions and no slang, and states claims objectively.

n.1: Slang ("skimp on," "tank") does not suit academic writing, even when a source is mentioned.
n.2: The contraction "don't" and the vague "enough" are informal and imprecise for a formal research paper.
n.3: Second person ("you") and a contraction ("You'd") are too conversational for a formal paper.

q: Jasmine is sending a quick text message to a close friend to confirm their lunch plans for today. Which message best fits this audience and purpose?
o: Please be advised that I will attend our scheduled lunch at noon.
Sounds good! See you at noon at the taco place.
Maybe lunch sometime this week? Let me know what works for you.
I am writing to confirm that I will meet you for lunch at noon today.
w: Register should match the audience. A text to a close friend is informal: short, friendly and conversational.

n.0: "Please be advised" is a formal business phrase that sounds cold in a message to a friend.
n.2: The casual tone fits, but the message fails the purpose: it does not confirm today's lunch plans.
n.3: "I am writing to confirm" is formal letter language, too stiff for a quick text to a close friend.

q: Andre is writing a cover letter to the human resources department of a regional hospital. Which sentence is most appropriate for this letter?
o: I am eager to bring my CNA experience to your medical-surgical unit.
I'm really excited about this job, and I know I'd be a great fit.
I am, without question, the most qualified applicant you will receive.
I need a full-time job with good benefits, and your hospital offers both.
w: A cover letter calls for a formal, confident and respectful tone that links the applicant's experience to the employer's needs.

n.1: The contractions and the vague "great fit" are too casual and give the employer no specific reason to hire.
n.2: The boastful claim sounds arrogant and cannot be supported, which suits no professional application.
n.3: The sentence focuses on what the writer wants rather than what the writer offers the hospital.

q: A nurse manager is writing a formal report to a hospital's board of directors: "The pilot program cut readmissions by 12 percent, which is a pretty big deal for a unit of our size." Which phrase should be revised?
o: the pilot program
a pretty big deal
cut readmissions
by 12 percent
w: "A pretty big deal" is slang. A formal report needs precise wording such as "a significant improvement for a unit of our size."

n.0: "The pilot program" is a precise, standard name for a trial program.
n.2: "Cut readmissions" is clear and accurate; "cut" is a standard verb for a reduction.
n.3: "By 12 percent" is a specific, formal way to report the result.

q: A school nurse is making a sign to hang above the sink in a second-grade classroom. Which sentence is most appropriate for these readers?
o: Wash your hands with soap before you eat.
Wash your hands with soap prior to consuming food.
Perform hand hygiene before you eat.
Hand washing reduces the spread of germs.
w: Young readers need short sentences, simple everyday words and a clear action to take.

n.1: "Prior to consuming food" is formal wording that young children may not know.
n.2: "Perform hand hygiene" is health-care jargon that seven-year-old readers may not understand.
n.3: This states a general fact but does not tell the children what to do at the sink.

q: A patient is writing to a hospital billing office to dispute a charge. Which sentence best meets the purpose and the audience?
o: Please remove the $85 charge for the March 4 visit, which my insurer paid.
I am writing to you about some issues I have had lately with things on my bill.
Your careless office billed me $85 for March 4, though my insurer paid it.
Hey, quick thing: that $85 charge from March 4 should go, since insurance paid.
w: A dispute letter should be courteous and specific: name the charge, the date and the requested action.

n.1: The sentence is polite but vague; it never says which charge is wrong or what should happen.
n.2: The facts are specific, but calling the office "careless" is accusing and likely to make the reader defensive.
n.3: The facts are specific, but "Hey, quick thing" is too casual for a letter to a billing office.

q: Lucia is writing a personal statement for a nursing program's admissions committee. Which sentences are appropriate for this audience and purpose? Select all that apply.
o: My long-term goal is to work as a pediatric nurse in a rural clinic.
Nursing has been my dream for years, and I am super excited to start!
Without a doubt, I will be the strongest student your program has admitted.
Caring for my grandmother after her stroke showed me what skilled nursing looks like.
Volunteering at a hospice taught me to listen before I act.
w: A personal statement may use first person, but it must stay formal and purposeful. The correct sentences give specific experiences and goals in standard language.

n.1: The intensifier "super" and the exclamation point are too casual for an admissions committee, and the sentence gives no specific experience.
n.2: The boastful, unsupported claim is arrogant and does not suit a formal personal statement.

q: A clinic is updating a flyer for the general public: "Individuals experiencing dyspnea or diaphoresis should seek emergent evaluation." Which revision best suits this audience while keeping the meaning?
o: Persons with respiratory distress or diaphoresis require emergent care.
If you have trouble breathing or heavy sweating, get emergency care now.
If you feel a little bit off, you might think about seeing a doctor.
If you have dyspnea or heavy sweating, get emergency care now.
w: Two checks: the revision must use plain words a lay reader knows (trouble breathing, heavy sweating) and keep the message's urgency.

n.0: "Respiratory distress," "diaphoresis" and "emergent" are still medical jargon for lay readers.
n.2: This version loses the specific symptoms and the urgency, so it changes the meaning.
n.3: The urgency is kept, but "dyspnea" is still a medical term that lay readers may not know.

q: A nurse is ending an email to her unit manager that requests a change to next month's schedule. Which closing sentence is most appropriate?
o: Let me know ASAP, since I already told my family I'd be off that weekend.
Thanks in advance for approving this change to my schedule.
Thank you for considering my request; I am glad to discuss it at any time.
I trust you will approve this request, as I have certainly earned it by now.
w: A professional email closes courteously, thanks the reader and offers to follow up.

n.0: "ASAP" and the assumption that the request is already approved are too informal and presumptuous.
n.1: Thanking the manager in advance "for approving" assumes the answer and pressures the reader.
n.3: The demanding tone pressures the manager and is not respectful.

q: Read the paragraph from a student's research summary. (1) A recent study examined how evening screen time affects sleep in adolescents. (2) Teens who used their phones after 9 p.m. got a lot less sleep. (3) On average, they slept 48 minutes less than peers who did not use phones at night. (4) These findings suggest that limiting evening screen use may improve rest. Which sentence does not match the formal register of the paragraph?
o: Sentence 1
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 2
w: Sentence 2 uses informal wording ("teens," "got," "a lot less"). A formal version: "Adolescents who used their phones after 9 p.m. slept less."

n.0: Sentence 1 is formal: precise terms ("adolescents," "evening screen time") and an objective tone.
n.1: Sentence 3 is formal: it reports a specific figure in standard language.
n.2: Sentence 4 is formal: "suggest" and "may" state the conclusion with appropriate caution.

q: A hospital's community newsletter is announcing a new screening service. Which sentence uses respectful, person-first language?
o: The clinic now offers free foot exams for people with diabetes.
The clinic now offers free foot exams for diabetics in the area.
The clinic now offers free foot exams for diabetes victims.
The clinic now offers free foot exams for diabetes sufferers.
w: Person-first language names the person before the condition: "people with diabetes."

n.1: "Diabetics" labels people by their condition; person-first language puts the person first.
n.2: "Victims" frames people as helpless and defines them by their condition.
n.3: "Sufferers" assumes how people experience the condition and defines them by it.

q: A city health department is writing a press release about a safety event. Which sentence uses inclusive, gender-neutral job titles?
o: The firefighters and policemen met with the council chair.
The firefighters and police officers met with the council chair.
The firefighters and police officers met with the council chairman.
The firemen and police officers met with the council chair.
w: Bias-free writing uses titles that fit any gender: firefighter, police officer, chair or chairperson.

n.0: "Policemen" is a gendered title; the neutral term is "police officers."
n.2: "Chairman" is a gendered title; the neutral term is "chair" or "chairperson."
n.3: "Firemen" is a gendered title; the neutral term is "firefighters."

q: A student is writing up a chemistry lab for a formal report. Which sentence uses the most precise wording?
o: The sample was heated for 10 minutes until it reached 80 degrees Celsius.
The sample was heated briefly until it reached a high temperature.
The sample was heated for several minutes until it reached 80 degrees Celsius.
The sample was heated for 10 minutes until it became very hot.
w: Precise word choice gives exact, specific information. A lab report should state measured values, not vague impressions.

n.1: "Briefly" and "a high temperature" sound formal but give no measurable information.
n.2: The temperature is exact, but "several minutes" is vague; a lab report needs the measured time.
n.3: The time is exact, but "very hot" is vague; a lab report needs the measured temperature.

q: Mr. Brooks is writing a letter to a hospital about a long wait in its emergency department. Which sentence has the most appropriate tone for his purpose?
o: Thanks a lot for the lovely four-hour wait; I really enjoyed it.
I waited four hours with a broken wrist and would like to know why.
I am sure the department was busy, so please disregard my concerns.
Your staff obviously could not care less about patients like me.
w: A complaint letter should be firm, specific and courteous: state what happened and what you want.

n.0: Sarcasm is unprofessional and can be misread, so it weakens the complaint.
n.2: This polite sentence cancels the complaint, so it fails the writer's purpose.
n.3: The angry, accusing tone is likely to make the reader defensive rather than helpful.

q: Malik is writing an essay for a nursing scholarship. Which sentence avoids clichés and is most appropriate for this essay?
o: Working as a medical scribe taught me to document care accurately.
Working as a medical scribe taught me to think outside the box every day.
At the end of the day, I know deep down that nursing is my true calling.
After my scribe job, I expect nursing school to be a walk in the park.
w: Clichés are overused phrases. Specific, concrete statements make a stronger impression on a scholarship committee.

n.1: "Think outside the box" is a cliché; it does not say what the writer actually learned.
n.2: "At the end of the day" and "true calling" are clichés that add little specific meaning.
n.3: "A walk in the park" is a cliché, and it suggests the writer underestimates the program.

q: Read the sentence from a staff policy: "Staff should utilize the aforementioned procedure in order to facilitate patient egress." Which revision replaces the inflated wording with plain language and keeps the meaning?
o: Staff should use the procedure described above as needed.
Staff should use this procedure to help patients leave.
Staff should employ the stated procedure to facilitate patient egress.
Staff should use the aforementioned procedure to help patients leave.
w: Plain language replaces inflated words: utilize = use, facilitate = help, egress = leaving, in order to = to.

n.0: This version drops the purpose (helping patients leave), so it loses meaning.
n.2: "Employ," "facilitate" and "egress" are still inflated words for "use," "help" and "leave."
n.3: "Aforementioned" is still an inflated word; plain language would say "this procedure."

q: A nurse is writing a reference letter for a former nursing aide: "Ms. Alvarez was ___ about following every infection-control step." Which word completes the sentence with the most positive connotation?
o: persnickety
obsessive
meticulous
nitpicky
w: All four words describe close attention to detail, but only "meticulous" has a positive, professional connotation.

n.0: "Persnickety" is informal and suggests fussing over trivial details, a negative connotation.
n.1: "Obsessive" suggests an unhealthy fixation, a negative connotation in a reference letter.
n.3: "Nitpicky" is informal and suggests petty fault-finding, a negative connotation.

q: Read the sentence from a county health report: "The new program did a lot of good things for people in the area." Which revision replaces the vague words with specific ones?
o: The new program provided free flu shots to 2,300 county residents.
The new program did many helpful things for many people in the county.
The new program helped a large number of local people in several ways.
The new program was very beneficial in a number of important ways.
w: Precise writing replaces vague words (things, stuff, a lot) with specific facts: what was provided, to whom and how many.

n.1: "Many helpful things" is still vague; it does not say what the program did.
n.2: "A large number" and "several ways" are still vague; the sentence never says what was done or for how many.
n.3: "Beneficial in a number of important ways" sounds formal but gives no specific detail.

q: A nursing journal editor is checking sentences in a research article. Which sentences use bias-free language? Select all that apply.
o: The study enrolled 50 adults confined to wheelchairs.
The study included 40 people with epilepsy.
The study enrolled 50 adults who use wheelchairs.
The new nurse manager, a woman in her 30s, was surprisingly organized.
Each server at the hospital cafe received a holiday bonus.
w: Bias-free language puts the person first ("adults who use wheelchairs," "people with epilepsy") and uses gender-neutral titles ("server").

n.0: "Confined to wheelchairs" treats the wheelchair as a limit rather than a tool; use "who use wheelchairs."
n.3: Mentioning gender and age is unnecessary here, and "surprisingly" implies a stereotype.

q: A charge nurse must tell a coworker that a medication dose was charted at the wrong time. Which sentence has the most appropriate tone?
o: How could you possibly mess up something as basic as charting a dose?
Not to be picky, but charting is kind of a big deal, you know what I mean?
Someone on this shift, and I won't say who, charted a dose at the wrong time.
I noticed the 9 a.m. dose was charted at 11 a.m.; can we fix it together?
w: Professional feedback is specific, respectful and focused on solving the problem.

n.0: The scolding question is condescending and likely to make the coworker defensive.
n.1: The passive-aggressive, casual phrasing is vague and unprofessional.
n.2: Hinting instead of speaking directly is indirect and can feel like public blame.

q: A company memo is announcing job cuts at a medical billing office. Which sentence states the information most clearly and directly?
o: The company will eliminate 40 positions on March 1.
The company will reduce the size of its workforce in the coming months.
The company is exploring workforce optimization opportunities.
The company is rightsizing its human capital going forward.
w: Clear professional writing states facts directly. Euphemisms and jargon blur important information.

n.1: This is less evasive, but it gives no number of positions and no date, so it is not the clearest statement.
n.2: "Workforce optimization" is vague jargon; it does not say what will happen or when.
n.3: "Rightsizing its human capital" is a euphemism that hides the fact that jobs are being cut.

q: A student is summarizing a small pilot study in a formal paper: "The results ___ that patients who walked daily recovered faster." Which word is most accurate and appropriate?
o: confirm
prove
suggest
establish
w: Two checks: the word must be formal, and it must match the strength of the evidence. A small pilot study "suggests" a result.

n.0: "Confirm" presents the finding as verified, which one small pilot study cannot do.
n.1: One small pilot study cannot prove a conclusion; "prove" overstates the evidence.
n.3: "Establish" claims the finding is settled, which overstates what a small study shows.

q: A student has drafted these supporting details for a paragraph: walking lowers blood pressure; it improves mood; it requires no special equipment. Which sentence would make the best topic sentence?
o: Most people already own a good pair of shoes for walking outside.
Walking is a simple habit that offers several health benefits.
Walking can lower blood pressure in many adults who do it daily.
Running burns more calories per mile than walking at a slow pace.
w: A topic sentence states the main idea that all of the supporting details develop. Each detail is a benefit of walking, so the topic sentence names those benefits in general.

n.0: This sentence is a minor detail about shoes; it does not cover blood pressure, mood or equipment.
n.2: This sentence states only one of the three details, so it is too narrow to be the topic sentence.
n.3: This sentence shifts to running, which none of the supporting details discuss.

q: Read the paragraph from an infection-control newsletter. (1) Hand washing is one of the most effective ways to prevent infections in hospitals. (2) Washing for at least 20 seconds removes most germs from the skin. (3) Alcohol-based sanitizers work well when hands are not visibly dirty. (4) Many nurses say they prefer unscented soaps to scented ones. (5) Staff who clean their hands between patients protect everyone on the unit. Which sentence should be removed to improve the paragraph's unity?
o: Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 5
Sentence 4
w: Every sentence should support the topic sentence: hand hygiene prevents infections. Sentence 4 mentions soap, but a preference for unscented soap says nothing about preventing infection, so it breaks unity.

n.0: Sentence 2 explains how long to wash, which directly supports the topic of preventing infection.
n.1: Sentence 3 adds a second hand-hygiene method, so it supports the topic.
n.2: Sentence 5 explains who benefits from hand hygiene, so it supports the topic.

q: Read the paragraph: "Community gardens offer more than fresh vegetables. Neighbors who garden together get to know one another and share skills. Gardeners also get regular outdoor exercise, and families eat more produce when they help grow it." Which sentence best concludes the paragraph?
o: Some gardeners prefer raised beds because they are easier on the back and knees.
In short, a community garden builds both good health and neighborly ties.
Vegetables such as tomatoes and peppers need at least six hours of sun each day.
However, many cities now charge a yearly fee for each garden plot in the spring.
w: A concluding sentence sums up the main idea without adding new information. This one ties together the social, exercise and nutrition benefits.

n.0: This sentence adds a new, minor detail instead of wrapping up the main point.
n.2: This sentence adds a new gardening fact unrelated to the benefits the paragraph lists.
n.3: This sentence introduces a new idea (fees) that the paragraph has not developed.

q: Topic sentence: "Getting enough sleep helps nursing students perform better in class." Which sentence best supports this topic sentence?
o: In one survey, students who slept seven hours outscored those who slept five on exams.
Many nursing students work part-time jobs at hospitals while they are enrolled in school.
Coffee is one of the most popular drinks among college students across the country.
Some campus dormitories set quiet hours that begin at 10 p.m. on most weeknights.
w: Supporting sentences give evidence for the topic sentence. The survey links more sleep to higher exam scores, a direct measure of class performance.

n.1: This sentence is about student jobs; it does not show that sleep affects class performance.
n.2: This sentence about coffee does not support a claim about sleep and performance.
n.3: Quiet hours relate to sleep, but this sentence gives no evidence about performance in class.

q: A volunteer is writing a short guide for first-time blood donors. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: After the donation, rest for about 15 minutes and have a snack.
First, drink plenty of water the day before your appointment.
Next, eat a meal rich in iron a few hours before you arrive.
Following these steps can help you feel well during and after your visit.
Before you donate blood, a few simple steps can help you prepare.
w: The topic sentence introduces the steps. "First" and "Next" give the steps before donating, "After the donation" follows them in time, and the concluding sentence sums up the benefit of the steps.

q: Read the paragraph. (1) Telehealth visits have grown quickly over the past decade. (2) These video appointments can save patients long drives and time off work. (3) However, telehealth does not suit every patient. (4) People without reliable internet may struggle to connect. Where should this sentence be placed? "For example, a farmer who lives an hour from town can see a provider without leaving work."
o: After sentence 1
After sentence 3
After sentence 4
After sentence 2
w: An example belongs right after the claim it illustrates. The farmer shows how video visits save long drives and time off work (sentence 2).

n.0: The example is about saving travel and work time, not about how quickly telehealth has grown.
n.1: Placed here, the example would contradict the claim that telehealth does not suit every patient.
n.2: Placed here, a success story would contradict the point about people who struggle to connect.

q: Read the paragraph from a county health report. (1) In 2015, the county had one free clinic. (2) By 2020, it had three, plus a mobile health van. (3) Last year, two more clinics opened in rural towns. (4) Access to free health care in the county has grown steadily over the past decade. Which sentence is the topic sentence?
o: Sentence 2
Sentence 1
Sentence 4
Sentence 3
w: This paragraph moves from specific to general: the details come first, and sentence 4 states the main idea they support.

n.0: Sentence 2 is another specific detail about the number of clinics in 2020.
n.1: Sentence 1 is a specific detail (one clinic in 2015); being first does not make it the main idea.
n.3: Sentence 3 is a specific detail about last year's openings.

q: A student's paragraph argues that hospitals should serve healthier food in their cafeterias. Which sentence would best conclude the paragraph?
o: Some hospitals currently serve meals from national fast-food chains in their lobbies.
First, cafeterias should add more fresh vegetables and whole grains to each meal.
Hospital parking fees are another issue that deserves attention from administrators.
Healthier menus would let hospitals model the habits they urge patients to adopt.
w: A strong concluding sentence restates or extends the paragraph's main point without adding a new topic.

n.0: This sentence is a supporting detail, not a conclusion that wraps up the argument.
n.1: "First" signals the start of a list of supporting points, which belongs in the body of the paragraph.
n.2: This sentence introduces a new topic (parking) instead of closing the argument about food.

q: A student is writing a short narrative paragraph for a nursing school application. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: Last summer, Elena decided to earn her nursing assistant certificate.
Two weeks later, she started her first job at a nursing home.
When the course ended, she passed the state skills exam on her first try.
During the course, she practiced skills such as bed baths and safe transfers.
She enrolled in a six-week evening course at the community college.
w: The paragraph is in chronological order: the decision, enrolling, practicing during the course, passing the exam when it ended, and starting a job two weeks later.

q: Topic sentence: "Volunteering at a hospital can help students decide whether nursing is right for them." Which sentence would best develop this paragraph?
o: Nursing school tuition varies widely from one state to another across the country.
Volunteers see how nurses spend a shift, from charting to comforting families.
Hospital volunteers often wear colored vests or jackets so that visitors spot them.
Many hospitals ask volunteers to be at least 16 years old before they can apply.
w: Development means adding relevant support. Seeing a nurse's real workday is exactly what helps a student decide whether nursing fits.

n.0: Tuition is a different topic; the sentence does not develop the idea of testing out the career.
n.2: This detail about uniforms does not support the claim about choosing a career.
n.3: This fact is about volunteer rules, not about how volunteering helps a student decide on nursing.

q: Read the paragraph from a nutrition handout. (1) Dietary fiber offers several benefits for digestion. (2) It adds bulk to stool, which helps prevent constipation. (3) Many breakfast cereals come in colorful boxes designed to appeal to children. (4) Fiber also feeds helpful bacteria in the large intestine. (5) White bread usually costs less than whole-wheat bread at the store. (6) Foods such as beans, oats and berries are good sources of fiber. Which sentences should be removed to improve the paragraph's unity? Select all that apply.
o: Sentence 3
Sentence 5
Sentence 2
Sentence 6
Sentence 4
w: Sentence 3 (cereal box design) and sentence 5 (bread prices) mention foods but say nothing about fiber's digestive benefits or sources, so both break unity.

n.2: Sentence 2 gives a digestive benefit of fiber, which directly supports the topic sentence.
n.3: Sentence 6 tells readers where to find fiber, which supports the paragraph's purpose.
n.4: Sentence 4 gives a second digestive benefit of fiber, so it belongs.

q: A student is writing a paragraph organized from the least to the most important point. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: One benefit is simple: the rent and utility bills are split in half.
A roommate in the same program can also quiz you before major exams.
Most important, a roommate who knows long clinical days offers support when the work feels overwhelming.
Sharing an apartment with a classmate during nursing school has real advantages.
w: The topic sentence comes first. "One benefit" opens the list, "also" adds a second point, and "Most important" signals the final, strongest point in order-of-importance organization.

q: A unit manager's report reads: "The new scheduling app was supposed to reduce overtime. ___, overtime hours rose by 15 percent in its first month." Which transition best completes the passage?
o: Therefore
For example
However
Furthermore
w: The second sentence contrasts with the first: overtime was expected to fall but rose. "However" signals contrast.

n.0: "Therefore" signals a result, but rising overtime is not a result of the plan to reduce it.
n.1: "For example" introduces an illustration, but the second sentence reports an unexpected outcome.
n.3: "Furthermore" adds a similar point, but the second sentence contradicts the expectation in the first.

q: A clinic notice reads: "The clinic's only X-ray machine broke down on Monday morning. ___, patients who needed imaging were sent to the hospital across town." Which transition best completes the notice?
o: As a result
Similarly
In contrast
For instance
w: The broken machine caused patients to be sent elsewhere, a cause-and-effect relationship. "As a result" signals an effect.

n.1: "Similarly" signals a comparison, but the second sentence describes a consequence.
n.2: "In contrast" signals a difference, but sending patients elsewhere follows from the broken machine.
n.3: "For instance" introduces an example, but sending patients away is an effect, not an example.

q: A nutrition handout reads: "Some common foods are high in hidden sodium. ___, a single serving of some canned soups contains more than a third of the recommended daily limit." Which transition best completes the handout?
o: Nevertheless
For example
In conclusion
Likewise
w: Canned soup is a specific case of a food with hidden sodium, so the second sentence illustrates the first. "For example" introduces an illustration.

n.0: "Nevertheless" signals contrast, but the second sentence supports the first rather than opposing it.
n.2: "In conclusion" signals a summary, but the second sentence is a specific detail.
n.3: "Likewise" compares two similar ideas, but the soup is an instance of the first claim, not a parallel claim.

q: A wellness flyer reads: "Regular exercise strengthens the heart and lungs. ___, it can improve the quality of a person's sleep." Which transition best completes the flyer?
o: In other words
Conversely
Specifically
In addition
w: The second sentence adds another benefit of exercise. "In addition" signals addition.

n.0: "In other words" restates the same idea, but better sleep is a new point, not a restatement.
n.1: "Conversely" signals an opposite idea, but better sleep is another benefit, not an opposite.
n.2: "Specifically" narrows the previous idea, but sleep quality is not a detail of heart and lung strength.

q: A patient leaflet about a vaccine reads: "___ the vaccine can cause a sore arm, most patients find this side effect mild and brief." Which word or phrase best completes the sentence?
o: Because
Whenever
Unless
Although
w: The sentence concedes a drawback (a sore arm) and then plays it down. "Although" signals concession.

n.0: "Because" signals cause, but a sore arm does not cause the side effect to be mild.
n.1: "Whenever" signals time, which does not fit a possible side effect weighed against its mildness.
n.2: "Unless" signals a condition, which makes the sentence illogical.

q: A pharmacy newsletter is printing a short problem-and-solution paragraph. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: Many patients forget to take their evening medications.
Another option is a phone alarm set for the same time each night.
